Methods for loa objects

Source: R/methods.loa.R
loa-methods.Rd

Methods defined for objects returned from the agreement_limit function.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'loa'
print(x, digits = 4, ...)

# S3 method for class 'loa'
plot(
  x,
  geom = c("geom_point", "geom_bin2d", "geom_density_2d", "geom_density_2d_filled",
    "stat_density_2d"),
  delta = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'loa'
check(x, error.ratio = NULL, bias_line = c("adjusted", "expected"), ...)

Arguments

x

object of class loa as returned from a agreement_limit function.

digits

The number of digits to print.

...

further arguments passed through, see description of return value for details. agreement_limit.

geom

String naming the type of geometry to display the data points. Default is "geom_point". Other options include: "geom_bin2d", "geom_density_2d", "geom_density_2d_filled", and "stat_density_2d".

delta

The maximal allowable difference.

error.ratio

For check, an optional known ratio of the measurement error variances, var(error of x) / var(error of y), as in dem_reg(), on the analysis scale (the log scale with log_tf = TRUE). Used only with data_type = "simple"; see "Proportional bias diagnostic".

bias_line

For check, the second (dashed) line drawn on the proportional bias panel when the test is corrected for measurement error (replicates or error.ratio): "adjusted" (default), the error-adjusted slope, or "expected", the slope expected from unequal measurement error alone. The test is the same either way. See "Choosing bias_line".

Value

print

Prints short summary of the Limits of Agreement.

plot

Returns a plot of the limits of agreement.

check

Returns plots testing the assumptions of a Bland-Altman analysis. P-values for the normality, heteroskedasticity, and proportional bias tests are provided as captions to the plot. The proportional bias results are attached as the attribute "prop_bias", a data frame with the test (test, corrected, n, statistic, df, p.value, and p.uncorrected, the uncorrected Pitman-Morgan p-value), the observed slope of the differences on the means (slope_obs), the slope expected from unequal measurement error alone (slope_null) and the error-adjusted slope (slope_adj), the implied scale of y relative to x on the true values, beta = (2 - slope_adj)/(2 + slope_adj), the within-subject variances (sw2_x, sw2_y), and error.ratio. Columns that do not apply are NA.

Proportional bias diagnostic

The proportional bias panel of check() plots the differences (centred) against the means, on the analysis scale (the log scale for log-transformed data), whether or not the fit used prop_bias. Because cov(x - y, x + y) = var(x) - var(y), a slope of the differences on the means only shows that the two methods have unequal total variance; the test of the slope is the Pitman-Morgan test of equal variances. Unequal variances arise from a true proportional bias (y = a + b x with b not 1), but also from unequal measurement error or from a prior calibration of one method on the other (Bland & Altman, 1999; Hopkins, 2004). With one measurement per method these cannot be told apart, and check() says so when the test is significant.

What is tested depends on the design:

  • One measurement per method (data_type = "simple"): the Pitman-Morgan test (t on n - 2 df). With error.ratio, the Deming slope of y on x for that error ratio is tested against 1 instead (the test reported by dem_reg()). The error variances implied by the Deming fit give the slope expected from unequal error.

  • Replicates (data_type = "reps"): the test uses subject means and is corrected for unequal measurement error. The covariance of the subject-mean differences and sums is compared with its expected value without proportional bias, \(s^2_{wx}\overline{1/m_x} - s^2_{wy}\overline{1/m_y}\), from the pooled within-subject variances, rather than with zero. The standard error is a jackknife over subjects (re-estimating the within-subject variances) with n - 1 df. Only the difference of the error variances enters, so an occasion effect shared by both methods (linked replicates) cancels. Complete pairs of measurements are used.

  • Nested data (data_type = "nest"): the true value changes within a subject, so the error variances cannot be estimated; the slope is tested with a random-intercept model (likelihood ratio test) and is subject to the same limitation as one measurement per method.

Choosing bias_line

When the test is corrected for measurement error (replicates or error.ratio), the panel shows the observed least-squares slope (solid, with its confidence band, which is not corrected) and a second, dashed line chosen by bias_line. The test and its p-value are the same for both choices; only the picture differs.

  • "adjusted" (default): the error-adjusted slope, the slope of the differences on the means that would be seen without measurement error, 2(1 - beta)/(1 + beta) for y = a + beta x on the true values. Without proportional bias it is horizontal.

    • Pros: one simple rule (is the dashed line flat?); its slope gives beta, the size of the proportional bias, which is reported in the caption; it applies in the same way to replicates and error.ratio.

    • Cons: the test is of the covariance, not of this slope, so how far the line is from flat is not a direct picture of the test statistic; when the error variances are similar it lies on top of the observed line and is hard to see.

  • "expected": the slope expected from unequal measurement error alone, with no proportional bias. Without proportional bias the observed (solid) line should follow it.

    • Pros: the gap between the two lines is what is tested, so the picture matches the p-value; it shows directly how much of the observed slope unequal error can explain.

    • Cons: "the solid line should follow the dashed one" is harder to judge than "the dashed line should be flat"; the size of the proportional bias (beta) is not shown (it is in the "prop_bias" attribute).

Neither line shows its own uncertainty; use the p-value (and, for the size, beta) rather than judging the lines by eye, particularly with few subjects.

References

Bland, J. M., & Altman, D. G. (1999). Measuring agreement in method comparison studies. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 8(2), 135-160.

Hopkins, W. G. (2004). Bias in Bland-Altman but not regression validity analyses. Sportscience, 8, 42-46.
